questions.question: Which three fields does each node inside a Java LinkedList hold?
questions.explanation: LinkedList is doubly linked. Each private Node stores its element plus links to the previous and next node.

questions.question: What is the time cost of get(i) on a LinkedList with n elements?
questions.explanation: There is no array to index into. Java walks from the nearer end, which halves the walk but is still O(n).

questions.question: What does this print? LinkedList<String> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.add("A"); q.addFirst("B"); q.addLast("C"); System.out.println(q);
questions.explanation: A goes in first, B is linked before it, and C is linked after it, giving [B, A, C].

questions.question: What does this print? Deque<Integer> d = new LinkedList<>(); d.push(1); d.push(2); d.push(3); System.out.println(d.pop());
questions.explanation: push and pop both work at the head, so the list behaves as a stack and the last pushed value, 3, comes out first.

questions.question: Which interfaces does LinkedList implement that ArrayList does not?
questions.explanation: Both classes implement List. Only LinkedList implements Deque, which adds offer, poll, push and pop.

questions.question: A loop reads a 100,000-item LinkedList with for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) and list.get(i). Why is it very slow?
options: size() is recalculated by counting nodes
Each get(i) walks the chain again, so the loop costs O(n squared)
LinkedList copies itself on every get
The loop throws an exception halfway
questions.explanation: size() is a stored field and is fast. The walk inside every get(i) is the problem. A for-each loop walks the chain only once.

questions.question: What does this print? Queue<String> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.offer("X"); q.offer("Y"); q.poll(); System.out.println(q.peek());
questions.explanation: offer adds at the tail and poll removes the head X. peek then shows the new head, Y, without removing it.

questions.question: Why does new LinkedList<String>().getFirst() fail at run time?
options: It returns null, which is then printed
The list is empty, so it throws NoSuchElementException
questions.explanation: getFirst and removeFirst throw on an empty list. peekFirst and pollFirst return null instead.

questions.question: When is inserting into the middle of a LinkedList truly O(1)?
options: Only when the list has fewer than 10 items
When a ListIterator is already standing at that position
questions.explanation: Relinking is O(1), but add(index, item) must walk to the index first. An iterator already there skips the walk.

questions.question: Why does a LinkedList usually use more memory than an ArrayList with the same items?
options: Each item needs a separate node object with two extra links
It reserves a capacity of 10 up front
It keeps a hash table beside the nodes
questions.explanation: An ArrayList holds one reference per slot. A LinkedList wraps every element in a node that also carries prev and next links.
